title: FeDaL: Federated Learning for Time Series Foundation Models
one_liner: Train one time series model across different datasets by separating shared patterns from dataset-specific quirks.
lead: Time series models struggle when trained on mixed datasets—each dataset has its own measurement quirks and patterns that don't match other datasets. This paper does not centralize all data in one place. Instead, it treats each dataset as a separate participant in a federated learning setup (like a town council where each neighborhood keeps its data private but all contribute to a shared model). The trick: teach the model to learn patterns that work everywhere by removing the dataset-specific biases at two stages—once on each dataset locally, and again when combining everyone's progress.

problem.h2: Datasets have hidden quirks that leak into models
paras: When you train a time series model (a system that learns to understand patterns over time, like stock prices or weather) on data from multiple datasets, something breaks. Each dataset carries its own invisible flavor—energy measurements run at high frequency while weather runs at low frequency; one measures in Celsius, another in Fahrenheit. A naive approach trains one model on all of them mixed together, and the model memorizes these dataset-specific quirks instead of learning the real patterns.

The beginner tries pooling all datasets and training together on a single machine. But the model gets confused: it learns that 'high frequency means this pattern' and 'low frequency means that pattern,' so it cannot work on new datasets it has never seen. It learned the decoration, not the skeleton.

callout.html: Learn time series patterns that transfer across datasets without moving the data, by teaching the model to ignore dataset-specific biases.

steps.b: Each dataset removes its own bias
steps.text: Subtract out the dataset-specific flavor from each time window.
Each dataset learns patterns on its bias-removed copy without sending raw data anywhere.
Each dataset sends back the weight changes it learned, not the data.
Aggregate updates, then strip out dataset disagreements about pattern breaks.
Send updated model back to datasets. Repeat until the model stabilizes.

object.h2: The one thing that changes: dataset-agnostic representation
paras: The paper changes how the model's internal learned representation (the numbers it uses to understand patterns) forms during training. Instead of learning dataset-specific quirks, it learns by repeatedly filtering out what is unique to each dataset. The representation becomes dataset-agnostic—it works on any time series, regardless of measurement frequency or scale.

hidden.name: Dataset-level bias list
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity called dataset-level bias. It is not one number, but a list of adjustments—one for each position in time, one for each measurement scale. Think of it as a fingerprint: each dataset leaves a mark on the model through this bias list. The bias is the systematic difference between what the dataset's average pattern looks like and what the average pattern looks like across all datasets.

The paper estimates this bias by computing the mean of each hidden pattern layer (called a hidden state in neural networks—the intermediate numbers the model computes internally), weighted by a learned importance mask (the scale adjustment). It then uses this estimate to filter patterns: subtract the bias before training locally, add it back when combining datasets.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger dataset-specific bias. Highlights show temporal and pattern biases.

reads.html: Dataset bias is the measurement quirk each dataset adds. Energy and weather sound different because they measure at different speeds and scales. The paper filters this out.

Bias has two parts: temporal resolution bias (how fast the measurements tick) and scale bias (how big the numbers are). Computed as the mean of hidden internal states weighted by learnable scaling factors.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: decentralized training + dual bias removal
paras: The core insight: federated learning splits the problem into two layers. Each dataset keeps its data private and trains locally, so no raw data moves. But when combining everyone's progress at the server, the model would normally pick up on the differences between datasets (energy vs. weather, fast vs. slow). The paper cuts this short at two stages.

First, Domain Bias Elimination (DBE) happens on each dataset's local machine: before sending its learned updates back, the dataset subtracts out its own measurement quirks from the patterns. This is like asking each researcher to note their lab's systematic error and remove it from their findings before sharing. Second, Global Bias Elimination (GBE) happens at the server when combining updates from all datasets: when the model sees conflicting information about where patterns break (one dataset says 'patterns shift here,' another says 'no they don't'), the server smooths over these pattern-transition disagreements. This prevents the global model from memorizing the topology of how one dataset's patterns differ from another's. The result: the model learns the universal skeleton of time series patterns, not the dataset-specific decorations.

stages.s: Mixed dataset partition (energy, weather, web traffic, etc.)
Domain Bias Elimination (DBE): remove dataset measurement quirks
Global Bias Elimination (GBE): smooth pattern-transition conflicts
One foundation model for all time series

math.h2: The core equation: federated loss with bias elimination
math.words: The total loss to minimize is the sum of local losses across all datasets, weighted by how many time points each one has, minus a regularization term that penalizes dataset-specific biases.
math.equation: F(theta) = sum_i (n_i / n) * F_i(theta_i; D_i) - lambda * ||b_t + b_s||^2
symbols: total loss we want to make small
number of time points in dataset i
total time points across all datasets
prediction error on dataset i using weights theta_i
scale bias (different measurement units or ranges)
how hard to push against dataset-specific biases

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say we have 2 datasets: Energy (100 million time points) and Weather (50 million).
Energy loss F_1 = 0.08, weight n_1/n = 100/150 = 0.67. Contribution: 0.67 * 0.08 = 0.054.
Weather loss F_2 = 0.12, weight n_2/n = 50/150 = 0.33. Contribution: 0.33 * 0.12 = 0.040.
Bias penalty (Energy bias = 0.05, Weather bias = 0.03): lambda * (0.05 + 0.03)^2 = 1.0 * 0.0064 = 0.0064.
Final loss: 0.094 - 0.0064 = 0.0876. Model reduces its bias by pushing against it every step.

math.note: The first term is federated learning (each dataset contributes proportionally to how much data it has). The bias penalty term ensures the learned representation strips dataset-specific quirks.

charts.note: Model memorizes dataset quirks. Fails on new data.

charts.title: FeDaL (federated + bias removal)
charts.note: Model learns universal patterns. Transfers to new datasets.

items.html: If the bias list is not computed correctly, some dataset quirks slip through. For example, if temporal resolution bias is estimated only at coarse granularity, high-frequency energy patterns still carry a faint signature the model can exploit.

items.b: Pattern-transition bias still leaks during global aggregation.
items.html: If Global Bias Elimination (GBE) is not aggressive enough, the model learns where datasets disagree about when patterns shift (e.g., one says 'trends break at 3 PM,' another says '4 PM'). It memorizes these breaks instead of learning universal patterns.
If one dataset has 1000x more time points than another, its local bias dominates. The model may over-remove bias from small datasets and under-remove bias from large ones.

When bias removal is calibrated per dataset (using sample-count weighting) and pattern-transition artifacts are smoothed globally, the model learns dataset-independent patterns and transfers to new time series.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a federated time series foundation model on a toy dataset partition (e.g., split energy and weather into two 'clients'). Train the model across both, applying Domain Bias Elimination on each and Global Bias Elimination at the server. Compare three things: (1) a naive pooled model trained on all data at once, (2) a federated model without bias removal, and (3) FeDaL with both DBE and GBE. Evaluate all three on a held-out new time series (e.g., web traffic) that the model has never seen. The key metric is zero-shot transfer accuracy: how well the model predicts on the new dataset without retraining.
demo.closing: FeDaL's zero-shot transfer should be 15-25% better than naive pooling, because it learned universal patterns instead of dataset quirks.
